content: Menopause is often a challenging period for many women, characterized by symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal atrophy, and dryness. Additionally, postmenopausal women face an increased risk of developing osteoporosis. Interventions that can alleviate the severity and frequency of these symptoms are likely to enhance a woman’s overall well-being and quality of life. Hormone therapy has been shown to effectively manage menopausal symptoms, but it is associated with potentially serious adverse effects. Experimental studies suggest that black cohosh may serve as a biologically plausible alternative treatment for menopause. However, clinical studies investigating its effectiveness have yielded inconsistent results. The objective of this review was to assess the clinical effectiveness and safety of black cohosh (Cimicifuga racemosa or Actaea racemosa) in managing menopausal symptoms in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women. Relevant studies were identified through a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, up to March 2012. Additional information was sought from content experts and manufacturers of black cohosh extracts. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared orally administered monopreparations of black cohosh to placebo or active medications in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women. Two independent reviewers selected the trials, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Study authors were contacted to obtain missing information. Sixteen randomized controlled trials involving a total of 2,027 perimenopausal or postmenopausal women were included. All studies used oral monopreparations of black cohosh, with a median daily dose of 40 mg, for an average duration of 23 weeks. Comparators included placebo, hormone therapy, red clover, and fluoxetine. Outcomes assessed included vasomotor symptoms (e.g., hot flushes), vulvovaginal symptoms, overall menopausal symptom scores, and adverse effects. The analysis found no significant difference between black cohosh and placebo in reducing the frequency of hot flushes (mean difference of 0.07 flushes per day; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.43 to 0.56 flushes per day; P = 0.79; 393 women; three trials; moderate heterogeneity: I² = 47%) or in menopausal symptom scores (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.10; 95% CI -0.32 to 0.11; P = 0.34; 357 women; four trials; low heterogeneity: I² = 21%). In contrast, hormone therapy significantly reduced the frequency of daily hot flushes (three trials; data not pooled) and menopausal symptom scores (SMD 0.32; 95% CI 0.13 to 0.51; P = 0.0009; 468 women; five trials; substantial heterogeneity: I² = 69%). However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the heterogeneity between studies. Comparisons of black cohosh with other interventions, such as red clover or fluoxetine, were either inconclusive due to significant heterogeneity or insufficient data or showed no statistically significant differences. Similarly, evidence regarding the safety of black cohosh was inconclusive, primarily due to poor reporting in the included studies. There was insufficient data to analyze outcomes such as health-related quality of life, sexuality, bone health, vulvovaginal atrophic symptoms, and night sweats. None of the trials reported cost-effectiveness data. The overall quality of the included trials was unclear, largely due to inadequate reporting of study methods. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to support the use of black cohosh for managing menopausal symptoms. However, further research in this area is justified. Future studies should focus on improving the quality of trial reporting, particularly with respect to allocation concealment and the handling of incomplete outcome data. Additionally, the effects of black cohosh on other important outcomes, such as health-related quality of life, sexuality, bone health, night sweats, and cost-effectiveness, warrant further investigation.
